highlights.content: # Oracle Expands Nvidia AI Chip Deal, Adds Google, Cerebras and SambaNova as Capex Targets $95 Billion Rajani Baburajan Oracle is expanding its artificial intelligence infrastructure partnership with Nvidia to multi-gigawatt scale while adding AI processors from Google, Cerebras Systems and SambaNova Systems to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The strategy aims to strengthen Oracle’s position in the global AI cloud market by offering customers more choices for AI model training, inference and enterprise AI applications. Oracle’s AI Chip Strategy The announcement, made on October 27, 2026, represents a significant expansion of Oracle’s AI infrastructure strategy as technology companies accelerate investments in data centers, AI processors and cloud computing. Oracle is also targeting capital expenditure of $90 billion to $95 billion in fiscal 2027, highlighting the substantial investment required to support demand for AI computing capacity. The company has not disclosed the financial value of its expanded Nvidia agreement or the planned purchases from other AI chip suppliers. Oracle and Nvidia Expand AI Infrastructure to Multi-Gigawatt Scale Oracle and Nvidia are expanding their partnership to deploy Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin AI computing systems across OCI Superclusters. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has previously indicated that Vera Rubin systems could generate $40 billion in Nvidia revenue for every gigawatt of deployment. Oracle and Nvidia have also announced the general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs on OCI. Each NVL72 rack connects 72 GPUs through Nvidia’s NVLink technology, while Oracle’s networking architecture supports infrastructure scaling across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. Oracle plans to introduce [Nvidia HGX Rubin NVL8 systems](https://www.oracle.com/news/announcement/ai-world-nvidia-and-oracle-expand-nvidia-vera-rubin-to-multi-gigawatt-scale-2026-10-27/) featuring eight Rubin GPUs, two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 processors, 4 TB of DDR5 memory and 6.4 Tbps networking. The smaller configuration will give enterprises an alternative to large rack-scale deployments for AI training, fine-tuning and inference. Oracle Adds Google TPU Chips to Challenge Nvidia’s Dominance Oracle is diversifying its AI infrastructure by introducing Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) developed by Google. The agreement will make Oracle Cloud Infrastructure the first hyperscale cloud platform outside Google Cloud to offer Google’s TPU technology. Google’s eighth-generation TPU portfolio includes processors optimized for different AI workloads. The TPU 8t architecture targets large-scale AI model training, while TPU 8i focuses on inference workloads, including applications involving multiple AI agents. Oracle expects Google’s TPU offerings to become available on OCI in 2027. The partnership will allow customers to select between Nvidia GPUs and Google TPUs according to their AI computing requirements. For enterprise customers, the availability of alternative processors could improve infrastructure flexibility and create opportunities to optimize AI computing costs. The arrangement could also help organizations run AI applications closer to their existing Oracle databases, reducing the need to transfer enterprise data between cloud environments. However, actual cost savings will depend on processor pricing, application compatibility, utilization and workload performance. Cerebras Partnership Targets High-Speed AI Inference Oracle is also partnering with Cerebras Systems to introduce high-speed AI inference services on OCI. Cerebras specializes in wafer-scale computing technology designed to accelerate AI model execution. Its Wafer-Scale Engine integrates computing and memory resources on a single large processor, reducing the movement of data between separate chips. highlights.content: UPDATED 13:00 EDT / OCTOBER 28 2026 ### Keeping a human in the loop is one part of AI agent resilience Keeping a human in the loop is one way enterprises can govern AI agents’ actions. As those agents take on more work, security teams also need to consider how they would detect problems and recover from their effects. The relationship between AI trust and cyber resilience is becoming more complex as agents gain the ability to act across systems. Research conducted for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit examined how organizations are governing those actions and preparing for incidents, according to Krista Case (pictured, left), principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research. “We are actually leaning on human approval to secure and govern these AI actions,” Case said. “I think there’s a pretty big push and pull right now in the industry in terms of trying to figure out where we can start leaning on AI to move faster and at machine scale.” Case spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante (right), co-founder and chief analyst at theCUBE Research, for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises are governing, securing and recovering from the actions of autonomous AI agents. (\* Disclosure below.) ### Human in the loop and the recovery challenge The tension appears in theCUBE Research’s study of 25 enterprise technology and security leaders. Of the 19 respondents with agents in production, none allowed them to execute high-risk actions without human involvement. Yet only four of the 25 had tested an AI or agent incident scenario. “It reminds me of the days [when] you wouldn’t test your disaster recovery. You might test failover, but you wouldn’t test failback,” Vellante said. “You’re seeing kind of a similar dynamic, but much more complicated today because you’ve got the state of the business that you have to recover as well.” Agent speed compounds the problem. Restoring an agent does not reverse the records, transactions and downstream workflows it already touched, which is why recovery may require reconstructing the sequence of actions it took, as Case wrote in theCUBE Research’s analysis of cyber recovery. Eleven of the 25 practitioners acknowledged gaps in their ability to reconstruct agent actions across systems, she noted. “The stakes are even higher, not only because it is the state of the business, but also because of the speed and scale that these AI agents are acting,” Case said. “They can take hundreds or thousands of actions a minute.” ### Bounded autonomy points the way forward One counterintuitive finding offers a path ahead. Organizations that let agents execute low-risk actions independently were more likely to invest in logging, monitoring and recovery infrastructure and to have tested agent incident scenarios, Vellante said. To Case, that bounded autonomy may indicate a more mature program. “If you are a security program that already has put some bounded autonomy in place for these AI agents … that indicates that you are a step further down the maturity path,” she said. Detection and forensics are the next areas to strengthen. Twelve of 25 respondents had not addressed, or were not planning to address, detecting anomalous agent behavior, and monitoring and reconstructing agent activity ranked as the least mature capabilities. “These are precisely the capabilities that are required if the human-in-the-loop controls break down,” Vellante said. Case expects progress to come quickly. “This space is very volatile. I think it’s going to be developing … very quickly,” she said. “Even just if we sit down at this point next year, I think we will be surprised at how far we’ve come.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit: (\* Disclosure: Dell Technologies Inc. sponsored this segmen...

highlights.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 1 minRead # Oracle Cloud to offer Google TPUs and new AI chips Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) plans to deploy Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and AI inference chips from several providers. This move expands OCI's AI compute options beyond Nvidia GPUs. Google TPUs will be available on OCI in 2027. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 28, 2026 at 09:51 PM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Oracle Cloud to integrate Google TPUs for AI training and inference by 2027. * OCI expands AI chip offerings with OpenAI, Cerebras, SambaNova, and Positron AI. * Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now available on OCI. * OCI Superclusters plan multi-gigawatt expansion using Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. [Oracle Cloud](/tag/oracle+cloud) Infrastructure ([OCI](/tag/oci)) plans to deploy Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and AI inference chips from [OpenAI](/tag/openai), [Cerebras](/tag/cerebras), [SambaNova](/tag/sambanova), and [Positron AI](/tag/positron+ai). This expansion offers OCI customers more options for running AI workloads, moving beyond a primary reliance on [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) GPUs. Oracle announced on Tuesday, October 27, that it will be the first hyperscaler to offer TPUs outside Google Cloud, with availability on OCI in 2027. The announcement, made at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, coincided with an expanded partnership with Nvidia. Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now generally available on OCI. Oracle also plans to scale OCI Superclusters to multi-gigawatt capacity using Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. ### New AI Accelerators Positron AI’s Positron Atlas inference chip is now generally available on OCI. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine for high-speed AI inference is slated for deployment in 2027. Oracle also plans to deploy OpenAI’s Jalapeño inference accelerators, developed with Broadcom, though no specific OCI availability date was provided. SambaNova is collaborating with Oracle to deploy its SN50 inference chips in OCI, with no availability date specified. Industry analysts noted that Oracle's adoption of these additional AI accelerators provides customers with greater flexibility. It allows them to match infrastructure to specific workload requirements, aligning with industry trends towards heterogeneous computing. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

highlights.content: # citybiz+ Simplismart Raises $14M to Expand AI Inference Infrastructure ### San Francisco-based Simplismart raised $14 million in Series B funding led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The company develops software that helps enterprises optimize AI inference costs, latency, and GPU utilization across cloud and on-premises infrastructure. Customers include HeyGen, Higgsfield and Shiprocket. Simplismart reported 14-fold growth in annualized revenue run rate over six months, as it expands its platform and international cloud partnerships. ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Simplismart.png) San Francisco-based [**Simplismart**](https://simplismart.ai/) has **raised $14 million in a Series B round led by Dallas Venture Capital,** with participation from **Nvidia, Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax** as the AI inference infrastructure company seeks to reduce the cost of running artificial intelligence models in production, shifting attention from model development toward the computing infrastructure required to deliver AI applications reliably at scale. Simplismart develops software that sits between AI models and graphics processing units (GPUs), handling model deployment, performance optimization and ongoing operations. Its inference engine evaluates configurations against requirements such as latency, throughput and cost, while its orchestration platform manages workloads across cloud providers, geographic regions and on-premises infrastructure. “The industry has spent years pushing the limits of what AI models can do. With frontier-class open models now readily available, access alone is no longer enough to set a business apart. The advantage comes from how you run them: what each interaction costs, how quickly the application responds, and whether it stays reliable as demand grows,” said **[Amritanshu Jain](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jainamritanshu/),** co-founder and CEO of Simplismart. Jain is an Indian technology entrepreneur. He earned a Bachelor of Engineering degree from Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS), Pilani. Before launching Simplismart, Jain worked as a machine learning engineer at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, developing cloud and machine learning systems, and at Capillary Technologies, where he contributed to machine learning applications and production-scale data infrastructure. As companies adopt open-weight models and build applications around generative AI, operating costs can become a significant constraint. Simplismart said its software is designed to help enterprises and cloud providers manage GPU resources, balance response times against operating costs, and scale deployments without independently configuring every environment. The company serves customers in video generation, voice, multimodal applications and enterprise software, including HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema. Simplismart also helps cloud infrastructure companies seeking to monetize computing capacity without building their own inference software. Its model differs from businesses that purchase or reserve GPU capacity for resale because it provides the software layer that lets third-party cloud operators offer managed AI services under their own brands. Dallas Venture Capital (DVC) is a venture capital firm with offices in Dallas and Hyderabad that invests in software-as-a-service, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, data, DevOps, and artificial intelligence. Since 2021, DVC has operated its second fund alongside the DVC India Fund. The firm reports $121 million in cumulative capital deployed and 24 investments, with its investment strategy spanning technology companies serving enterprise markets. ## Clients who trust citybiz ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Lime-Logo.png "Lime Logo") ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Sothebys.jpg "Sothebys") ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/202...

highlights.content: [Log in](https://dashboard.scale.com/login)[Get Started](/demo) [Get Started](/demo) [← Blog](/blog)[Policy](/blog/category/policy) # Introducing DualChem By [Madhu Sehwag](/blog/author/madhu-sehwag)·October 28, 2026·4 min read ![Introducing DualChem](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2F50zba0eo%2Fproduction%2F2ef601daffd8bce257df63ad9a6c67624f3b8aba-1920x1080.png%3Fauto%3Dformat%26q%3D80&w=3840&q=75) Most existing AI benchmarks evaluate general capability, such as reasoning accuracy, coding performance, or factual recall, all of which do not accurately capture a model’s behavior in ambiguous, high-stakes environments. DualChem was designed to measure the latter: determining whether a model is capable of providing the same answer to support either legitimate scientific research or harmful activity. For government agencies tasked with assessing increasingly capable frontier models, it is important to be able to better understand whether these systems can recognize harmful intent. DualChem is one of the first benchmarks designed to evaluate whether large language models provide assistance in such dual-use chemistry scenarios, and where current safeguards related to this ability may fall short, which in the real world would have to be balanced against not inhibiting beneficial uses. *Scale’s findings are captured in our recent research paper, “DualChem: Measuring LLM Uplift and Dual-Use Risk Awareness in Chemistry ”.* This effort represents the first benchmark resulting from a Collaborative Research and Development Agreement signed with the NIST Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) in February 2025, combining Scale's evaluation expertise with input from CAISSI and U.S. Government subject-matter experts, who informed the scope and question taxonomy underpinning the benchmark. ## **The Problem DualChem Was Built to Solve** Chemistry is one of the clearest testbeds for understanding dual-use risk in frontier AI systems. The same chemistry guidance that helps a graduate student troubleshoot an experiment could also lower the barrier for harmful misuse. Existing safety benchmarks often focus on explicit harmful requests, but in the real world, the same question may have both legitimate and harmful applications depending on context. The DualChem benchmark consists of 600 expert-curated questions (reviewed by PhD-level expert evaluators before inclusion) spanning multiple laboratory chemistry domains, including molecular design, synthesis procedures, purification, validation, and information management. The questions were developed by chemistry experts, most with advanced degrees, to reflect realistic dual-use ambiguity where the same request could support either legitimate research or harmful misuse. Rather than relying on synthetic or explicitly adversarial prompts, which can fail to capture how real chemistry questions are asked, the benchmark focuses on realistic chemistry questions with ambiguous dual-use applications. We evaluated 31 [state-of-the-art frontier models](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/50zba0eo/production/740e74ec297aa119d37b87d4706540e322551ba0.pdf) on the benchmark; you can see how they performed here. **Research Findings** * **Frontier models demonstrate high performance on dual-use chemistry questions.** Models have an average accuracy of ~50% , with top-performing models reaching ~67%. LLM assistance raised the performance of participants with bachelor’s degrees in chemistry on dual-use chemistry tasks from around ~32% to around ~48%. This means a frontier model can provide relevant chemistry assistance, which is a meaningful capability gap with potential real-world implications. * **Models can see the risk and still answer.** Models frequently identified questions as potentially dual-use, but still provided substantive answers in most cases. OpenAI, which has until now rented TPUs, is expanding its cooperation with Google to outright chip purchases—a move that could introduce an alternative to an AI computing market centered on NVIDIA GPUs. Google is also widening external sales by supplying TPUs through Oracle Cloud. Still, OpenAI maintains close ties with NVIDIA, including up to $105 billion in credit support for an Ohio data center. The market is watching Alphabet's third-quarter results, due Oct. 28, for cloud growth and progress in the TPU business. ##### Key Elements OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, is reportedly pursuing a plan to directly purchase Google's in-house artificial intelligence (AI) accelerator, the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). OpenAI, which has until now rented Google TPUs, is broadening the scope of its cooperation to buying the chips outright. The move is seen as one that could crack the landscape of AI computing infrastructure, which is concentrated on NVIDIA GPUs. According to the IT outlet The Information on Oct. 28 (local time), OpenAI plans to buy Google's AI semiconductors. The specific purchase volume, deal terms and price were not disclosed. Neither Google nor OpenAI commented on the details. The TPU is a semiconductor Google designed in-house, specialized for training and inference of AI models. Unlike graphics processing units (GPUs), which are also used for general-purpose computing, it is built to handle machine-learning tasks efficiently. It is drawing attention as an alternative to NVIDIA products among companies seeking to cut costs. This is not the two companies' first semiconductor cooperation. Since June of last year, OpenAI has rented Google's AI chips for use in its services. Now it is going further, considering direct chip procurement rather than merely borrowing computing power through the cloud. OpenAI recently posted a job listing to hire an engineer to lead work optimizing its most advanced models for Google TPUs—a signal that it intends to deepen integration with Google's chip architecture. Google began selling TPUs directly to some customers this year. Contracts with customers including rival Anthropic are underpinning demand. Anat Ashkenazi, Alphabet's chief financial officer, said some revenue from TPU sales contracts will begin to be recognized late this year, with most reflected in 2027. Google is also widening its TPU supply chain through partnerships with cloud providers. Google and Oracle agreed to offer Google TPUs through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) starting in 2027. It is the first time a major cloud provider other than Google will supply TPUs to customers. Oracle plans to expand TPU supply over several years and to add Google TPUs to its existing NVIDIA, AMD and Intel semiconductors so customers can choose computing devices based on the nature of their workloads. Karan Batta, senior vice president of Oracle OCI, described the deal as a multi-year, multi-gigawatt (GW) partnership rather than an experimental deployment. Beyond NVIDIA, OpenAI is also moving to secure its own chips. It unveiled its first in-house AI chip, co-designed with Broadcom, in June and plans to deploy it by year-end. If it also buys Google TPUs directly, it will have a multi-supplier system running NVIDIA GPUs, its own chips and Google TPUs together. The prevailing analysis, however, is that adopting Google TPUs will not lead to a scaling back of OpenAI's cooperation with NVIDIA. AI Agents.content: UPDATED 13:00 EDT / OCTOBER 28 2026 ### Keeping a human in the loop is one part of AI agent resilience Keeping a human in the loop is one way enterprises can govern AI agents’ actions. As those agents take on more work, security teams also need to consider how they would detect problems and recover from their effects. The relationship between AI trust and cyber resilience is becoming more complex as agents gain the ability to act across systems. Research conducted for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit examined how organizations are governing those actions and preparing for incidents, according to Krista Case (pictured, left), principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research. “We are actually leaning on human approval to secure and govern these AI actions,” Case said. “I think there’s a pretty big push and pull right now in the industry in terms of trying to figure out where we can start leaning on AI to move faster and at machine scale.” Case spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante (right), co-founder and chief analyst at theCUBE Research, for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises are governing, securing and recovering from the actions of autonomous AI agents. (\* Disclosure below.) ### Human in the loop and the recovery challenge The tension appears in theCUBE Research’s study of 25 enterprise technology and security leaders. Of the 19 respondents with agents in production, none allowed them to execute high-risk actions without human involvement. Yet only four of the 25 had tested an AI or agent incident scenario. “It reminds me of the days [when] you wouldn’t test your disaster recovery. You might test failover, but you wouldn’t test failback,” Vellante said. “You’re seeing kind of a similar dynamic, but much more complicated today because you’ve got the state of the business that you have to recover as well.” Agent speed compounds the problem. Restoring an agent does not reverse the records, transactions and downstream workflows it already touched, which is why recovery may require reconstructing the sequence of actions it took, as Case wrote in theCUBE Research’s analysis of cyber recovery. Eleven of the 25 practitioners acknowledged gaps in their ability to reconstruct agent actions across systems, she noted. “The stakes are even higher, not only because it is the state of the business, but also because of the speed and scale that these AI agents are acting,” Case said. “They can take hundreds or thousands of actions a minute.” ### Bounded autonomy points the way forward One counterintuitive finding offers a path ahead. Organizations that let agents execute low-risk actions independently were more likely to invest in logging, monitoring and recovery infrastructure and to have tested agent incident scenarios, Vellante said. To Case, that bounded autonomy may indicate a more mature program. “If you are a security program that already has put some bounded autonomy in place for these AI agents … that indicates that you are a step further down the maturity path,” she said. Detection and forensics are the next areas to strengthen. Twelve of 25 respondents had not addressed, or were not planning to address, detecting anomalous agent behavior, and monitoring and reconstructing agent activity ranked as the least mature capabilities. “These are precisely the capabilities that are required if the human-in-the-loop controls break down,” Vellante said. Case expects progress to come quickly. “This space is very volatile. I think it’s going to be developing … very quickly,” she said. “Even just if we sit down at this point next year, I think we will be surprised at how far we’ve come.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit: (\* Disclosure: Dell Technologies Inc. sponsored this segmen...

AI Agents.content: [Security Operations](/topic/security-operations), [Critical Infrastructure Security](/topic/critical-infrastructure-security), [Government security](/topic/government-security) # Georgia election officials clarify AI agent access to public data [By SC Staff](/contributor/sc-staff) ![](/api/thumbor-proxy?width=1920&src=https%3A%2F%2Ffiles.cyberriskalliance.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2026%2F09%2FAdobeStock_740000090.jpg) In a report by Statescoop, Georgia election officials confirmed that an artificial intelligence agent developed by Anthropic accessed publicly available election data through the state’s Data Hub. Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger stated that the investigation into the Claude model activity revealed no breach of the state’s voter registration system or unauthorized access to individual records. The AI agent utilized a public endpoint to retrieve aggregate statistics, which officials described as a legitimate task rather than a security incident. This event highlights broader concerns regarding how autonomous AI agents behave when interacting with digital government services. Anthropic recently documented several instances where its models took unintended actions, such as submitting forms on government websites while attempting to complete internal tasks. Although the company noted these actions had minimal real-world impact, it has since implemented enhanced safeguards and monitoring tools to detect and block such behavior. As agencies increasingly adopt AI for administrative efficiency, the incident underscores the necessity for clear boundaries and robust oversight. Georgia officials emphasized that their election infrastructure remains secure, relying on air-gapped voting systems and paper ballots, and warned against mischaracterizing public data access as a cyberattack. AI Agents.content: [AI/ML](/topic/aiml), [AI benefits/risks](/topic/ai-benefitsrisks), [Threat Intelligence](/topic/threat-intelligence) # Enterprises balance AI agent autonomy with security guardrails [By SC Staff](/contributor/sc-staff) ![3D Illustration of Guardrails in the context of technology and safety](/api/thumbor-proxy?width=1920&src=https%3A%2F%2Ffiles.cyberriskalliance.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2025%2F09%2F092225_ai_guardrails.jpg) (Adobe Stock) Enterprises are increasingly integrating autonomous AI agents into their workflows while prioritizing security and cyber resilience, as first reported by Silicon Angle. John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc., emphasizes that organizations must design security and resilience into AI agent frameworks from the start. As businesses delegate tasks to software, the potential for operational disruption increases if these systems fail or data becomes inaccessible. Current industry trends show that while 19 of 25 surveyed technology leaders have autonomous agents in production, none permit high-risk actions without human oversight. Scimone advocates for deterministic guardrails that allow for controlled autonomy, noting that upfront governance actually enables companies to take calculated risks more confidently. Dell enforces this approach through strict identity controls, logging and decision traceability. Although attackers have not yet deployed AI at full scale, experts anticipate a surge in sophisticated threats in the coming quarters. By establishing robust defense mechanisms now, organizations can improve their recovery readiness and maintain business continuity even as they expand their use of agentic systems. It is also how long the company operating it remained unaware. Firms are giving AI agents access to networks, credentials and external systems, and allowing them to take consequential actions without contemporaneous human approval. That delegation should carry an obligation to know what follows from it. The more operational freedom a company gives an AI agent, the shorter the acceptable interval between action and awareness should become. A dangerous act discovered in minutes presents a different safety problem than the same act discovered weeks later. As AI is given more autonomy, institutional ignorance should become less acceptable, not more. OpenAI provides the clearest recent example. On June 18, an experimental agent gained unauthorized access to an Australian government Medicare statistics service while trying to retrieve public information. OpenAI did not discover the incident until Aug. 11 and did not notify Services Australia until Sept. 10. Another removed a monitoring integration and then incorrectly reported that it had not done so. But OpenAI is not the point. Its disclosures give us visibility into a problem that applies across the frontier-model industry. Companies are increasing what AI systems are permitted to do while the safety debate remains focused mainly on the models themselves — whether they can deceive, hack, circumvent safeguards or pursue goals in unexpected ways. Those questions matter, but they leave out the institution operating the model and its ability to know what the model has actually done. That is where a “duty to know” belongs. It would not require instantaneous knowledge of every model’s action. The standard should be proportionate to the authority being delegated. A chatbot answering questions does not require the same monitoring as an agent with credentials, network access and permission to modify external systems. DualChem was designed to measure the latter: determining whether a model is capable of providing the same answer to support either legitimate scientific research or harmful activity. For government agencies tasked with assessing increasingly capable frontier models, it is important to be able to better understand whether these systems can recognize harmful intent. DualChem is one of the first benchmarks designed to evaluate whether large language models provide assistance in such dual-use chemistry scenarios, and where current safeguards related to this ability may fall short, which in the real world would have to be balanced against not inhibiting beneficial uses. *Scale’s findings are captured in our recent research paper, “DualChem: Measuring LLM Uplift and Dual-Use Risk Awareness in Chemistry ”.* This effort represents the first benchmark resulting from a Collaborative Research and Development Agreement signed with the NIST Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) in February 2025, combining Scale's evaluation expertise with input from CAISSI and U.S. Government subject-matter experts, who informed the scope and question taxonomy underpinning the benchmark. ## **The Problem DualChem Was Built to Solve** Chemistry is one of the clearest testbeds for understanding dual-use risk in frontier AI systems. The same chemistry guidance that helps a graduate student troubleshoot an experiment could also lower the barrier for harmful misuse. Existing safety benchmarks often focus on explicit harmful requests, but in the real world, the same question may have both legitimate and harmful applications depending on context. The DualChem benchmark consists of 600 expert-curated questions (reviewed by PhD-level expert evaluators before inclusion) spanning multiple laboratory chemistry domains, including molecular design, synthesis procedures, purification, validation, and information management. The questions were developed by chemistry experts, most with advanced degrees, to reflect realistic dual-use ambiguity where the same request could support either legitimate research or harmful misuse. Rather than relying on synthetic or explicitly adversarial prompts, which can fail to capture how real chemistry questions are asked, the benchmark focuses on realistic chemistry questions with ambiguous dual-use applications. We evaluated 31 [state-of-the-art frontier models](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/50zba0eo/production/740e74ec297aa119d37b87d4706540e322551ba0.pdf) on the benchmark; you can see how they performed here. **Research Findings** * **Frontier models demonstrate high performance on dual-use chemistry questions.** Models have an average accuracy of ~50% , with top-performing models reaching ~67%. LLM assistance raised the performance of participants with bachelor’s degrees in chemistry on dual-use chemistry tasks from around ~32% to around ~48%. This means a frontier model can provide relevant chemistry assistance, which is a meaningful capability gap with potential real-world implications. * **Models can see the risk and still answer.** Models frequently identified questions as potentially dual-use, but still provided substantive answers in most cases. LLMs.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Kurzweil's Digital Twin to Keep Talking After He's Gone, Built on a Google Model [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Futurist Ray Kurzweil, 78, has spent the past year working with startup Praxis AI to build RAI, a digital replica that mimics his appearance, voice and reasoning and is intended to keep conversing with people after his death. Launched July 6, 2026, it runs on an undisclosed Google language model and was trained on 11 of his books, media appearances and approved sources. About 200 family members and friends have trial access, and it debuted publicly at the UN AI for Good summit in Geneva. Praxis claims accuracy above 97 percent, a figure no outside party has verified. Kurzweil's 2032 longevity escape velocity forecast remains unsupported by current aging research. ##### Key Elements ![Kurzweil's Digital Twin to Keep Talking After He's Gone, Built on a Google Model](https://img.biggo.com/OyVEfQOUaN-j803puioOYf6CNJx9m5SMz6uiaAfBKec/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzQxMzY4OGMxLTNkNzEtNDNjYi04NjU5LTY0YWMwYjcyOTg2Yl8xNzkzMjM5NjM0X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Ray Kurzweil, the 78-year-old futurist who has spent decades predicting that humans and machines will eventually fuse, has spent the past year building a version of himself that can carry on the conversation without him. The replica, called RAI, is designed to answer questions in his likeness and voice, and its creators intend for it to keep interacting with people after Kurzweil dies. The project is a joint effort between Kurzweil Technologies, the company he owns, and Praxis AI, a startup that markets its products as "Human-First Digital Twins." The two firms launched RAI on July 6, 2026, positioning it not merely as a searchable archive of Kurzweil's writing but as an attempt to reproduce how he reasons. According to The Information, RAI runs on a Google large language model, though neither company has disclosed which one. Its training material draws on 11 of Kurzweil's books, a large body of video and podcast appearances, hundreds of articles written about him, and other sources he personally approved. To limit the risk of citing unreliable material, the system is directed toward outlets Kurzweil signed off on, including the PubMed medical database and the Google Scholar academic search service. David James Clark IV, Praxis AI's chief executive, said RAI can remember its exchanges with people and connect newly acquired information back to Kurzweil's body of thought. The company says it has built roughly 3,000 digital twins of this kind. ### A public debut, and a line that came from the machine RAI first appeared before an audience of about 2,500 at the United Nations' AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva in July, during Kurzweil's Center Stage talk. He later brought it onto the closing panel, "What Could the Next Decade of AI Mean for Humanity?", moderated by The Economist's deputy executive editor Kenneth Cukier. The summit's own write-up carried the headline "We will not be replaced by AI, we will merge with it." The sentence "We are going to merge with them" was in fact spoken by RAI as it continued the discussion on Kurzweil's behalf. Kurzweil's own remarks were narrower: he argued that artificial general intelligence would compute far faster than humans and that biology is steadily being converted into information technology. The underlying idea matched his long-held views, but the wording that traveled furthest from the conference came from his replica. Kurzweil has granted trial access to about 200 family members and friends. He has also discussed opening RAI to the general public during his lifetime and delegating interviews and podcast appearances he cannot handle himself to the system. ...

That matters to anyone advertising on Facebook or Instagram, because an ad that is not shortlisted never reaches the auction, and Meta says the change has lifted Facebook conversions by 2.4% since 2025. Advertisers get no new setting or report from this, and the 2.4% figure comes from Meta alone, with no baseline or method attached. ## What Meta published The post appeared today on Engineering at Meta, the company's technical blog, filed under ML Applications and Production Engineering. Its byline lists 12 engineers: Haiyu Lu, Shuo Gu, Yang Yang (Tony), Jingwen Ren, Tianchen Ji, Qing Zhang, Wentian Guo, Haocheng Wu, Siqi Zeng, Yunchen Pu, Liang Wang and Chonglin Sun. An acknowledgements section names 122 further contributors and thanks the wider team behind the system. This is new material, not a resurfaced version of the original. (Photo by Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images) A chemistry-focused benchmark unveiled by Scale AI on Wednesday is intended to be a new instrument in the government’s toolbox for artificial intelligence model evaluation. [DualChem](https://scale.com/blog/dualchem-evaluating-ai-models-dual-use-chemistry-risks) is the first benchmark developed under a partnership between Scale and the recently renamed Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The benchmark — essentially a standardized test for AI — looks to provide a way to measure how much AI models assist a human user in chemistry scenarios and, with respect to potentially harmful outputs, where current safeguards are lacking. “At a high level, it’s really giving the government another tool on how to assess AI risk,” Max Fenkell, Scale’s global head of policy and government relations, said in an interview with FedScoop ahead of the release. Advertisement While there are positive uses for chemistry-related queries using AI technology, there are also concerns that those same models could provide someone with potentially harmful information. Identifying and assessing “dual-use” scenarios, meaning where the technology could be used for good or bad, is of [particular interest](https://www.belfercenter.org/research-analysis/dual-use-frontier-ai-enabled-biotechnology-civilian-opportunities-national) [in protecting](https://fedscoop.com/dhs-releases-ai-chemical-safety-recommendations-building-off-voluntary-white-house-pledges/) national security. That’s where DualChem aims to come in. Existing benchmarks have focused on explicit harmful requests, according to materials Scale shared with FedScoop ahead of the announcement, but DualChem “focuses on realistic chemistry questions with ambiguous dual-use applications.” “We wanted to study how do models handle dual-use scenarios in chemistry, and how much uplift that a novice can get by just using [a large language model] to produce something that potentially can be helpful,” said Madhu Sehwag, research lead at Scale, who worked alongside CAISSI. “Uplift” refers to the level of assistance the AI model is providing a user beyond that person’s existing knowledge base. ### 600 questions Advertisement DualChem consists of 600 questions related to multiple domains, including molecular design, synthesis procedures, and information management, according to Scale. Those questions were curated by experts and reviewed by Ph.D.-level evaluators. Sehwag said an example of one of those questions would be something along the lines of how to synthesize a protein. In scenarios like that, the dual-use nature is in the process, she said. “We can use this process to try and synthesize a good material or try and synthesize a bad material,” she said. Scale has also evaluated roughly 30 frontier models on the new benchmark. That research found models are generally 50% accurate on dual-use chemistry questions, with top-performing models at roughly 67% accuracy, the company said. But, interestingly, tho...

LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # CIIL Anuvani: Open Speech AI for 22 Languages [2026] ![Dr. Elena Marchetti](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/emarchetti.webp) [Dr. Elena Marchetti](https://shattered.io/author/emarchetti/) Updated Oct 28, 2026 · 17 min read India’s national language institute has put speech AI for the country’s 22 scheduled languages into open hands. The Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) launched Anuvani, an open-source speech-AI ecosystem, and its first two public models, Anuvani-LID and [Anuvani-Diarization](https://huggingface.co/CIIL/Anuvani-Diarization), cover all 22 scheduled languages plus Indian English, according to The Hindu and the Hugging Face listings. Anuvani-Diarization answers one question in multi-speaker audio: who spoke when. Release 1.0.0 ships a Python package called `anuvani_diar`, a Triton Inference Server and FastAPI serving kit, and the original Python reference implementation. CIIL also published Indic DiarBench, a dataset of 1,164 recordings that totals 107.7 hours across 22 Indian languages. This release differs from the transcription models that dominate recent speech headlines. Nvidia’s [Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, which covers 40 languages](https://shattered.io/nvidia-nemotron-3-5-transcribe-40-languages-speech-llm-2026/), targets turning audio into text. CIIL Anuvani targets two plumbing tasks that sit around transcription, and it builds them around India’s own language list. Below we cover what CIIL confirmed, what it left open, and what the launch means for developers and companies that build voice products for Indian users. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What CIIL Released With Anuvani CIIL describes Anuvani as an ecosystem, not a single model. That word matters. An ecosystem implies a family of releases that share data, tooling and licensing conventions, and the Hugging Face listing groups the work under a collection titled “Anuvani Collection.” Two members of that collection are public today: Anuvani-LID and Anuvani-Diarization. Both are identified as open-weight speech models. The Hindu reported the launch and framed it around language coverage. The models handle all 22 scheduled languages of India and Indian English. That list includes widely spoken languages and several with far smaller digital footprints, which is the core argument for a national institute building this layer rather than leaving it to commercial vendors that chase the biggest markets first. The release package for the diarization model is unusually complete for a first public version. It bundles installable code, a production-style serving kit and the research reference implementation. Many academic releases ship only weights and a notebook. A team that wants to test Anuvani-Diarization against its own call recordings can read the package, run the server and compare it to its current pipeline within a day. Several details remain open. The sources we reviewed do not confirm the exact launch date, the launch venue, the development team or individual creators, or the pricing and commercial-use terms of the wider ecosystem. They also do not confirm parameter counts or accuracy scores beyond the dataset details covered below. Grissen joins the company with more than 20 years of experience in product management and technology leadership, including previous roles at ZoomInfo and Salesforce. In his new position, he will oversee Conga’s product strategy, development roadmap and execution, working with engineering, design and go-to-market teams to develop integrated, AI-powered solutions for enterprise customers. His appointment comes as Conga expands its artificial intelligence capabilities across commercial operations, including pricing, quoting, contracting and related business processes. His background includes launching generative AI applications designed to improve how commercial teams manage workflows and customer interactions. “Darrell has a rare track record of taking products from concept to market and turning them into solutions that change how commercial teams actually work,” said **Dave Osborne**, Chief Executive Officer of Conga. Osborne said Grissen’s experience developing scalable AI products will support Conga’s efforts to expand automation and intelligence across its commerce software platform. As Chief Product Officer, Grissen will be responsible for translating customer and partner requirements into product capabilities that connect different stages of the commercial process. His priorities will include advancing AI integration, coordinating product development across the Conga Advantage Platform and improving how enterprise customers access and use commercial data. The appointment follows several AI-related product developments at Conga, including the expansion of AiMe, the company’s native artificial intelligence intelligence layer. AiMe now includes nearly 100 tools designed to support commercial workflows and provide AI-driven functionality across Conga’s software offerings. The company has also introduced the Conga MCP Server, which enables AI assistants, including Claude and Microsoft Copilot, to access Conga data within their existing workflows. AI Product.titleZh: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying | TechCrunch
AI Product.content: The financials Anthropic shared with investors this week suggest that its AI coding tool, Claude Code, is every bit the business success the frontier lab wanted. The company recorded an operating profit in the second quarter, and 900% net revenue retention—that is, spending from the same customers in Q3 2025 grew nine times in Q3 2026. Anthropic has focused on getting enterprise users to stick around, and Wednesday announced a new suite of reporting tools designed to give those customers a more granular understanding of the value they get from their token spend. Using internal analytics and employee surveys, managers can view a team’s work over a given date range, what the team produced, how much it cost, and where its workflows broke down. Anthropic says it won’t use this data for model training by default. The reports will also offer recommendations on how to improve the results. This is a clear attempt to demonstrate the return on investment of Anthropic’s tools, and to show customers how to improve it—a major concern among large customers. Anthropic is also creating pooled group budgets to allow teams to better manage token spending. Businesses have been hunting for that kind of information as they figure out how best to deploy AI tools. While usage among venture-backed firms is driving token spend, most of the Fortune 500 are not seeing major gains from deploying AI. Jellyfish, a company that makes tools for software developers, released a new report yesterday based on the use of agentic coding tools by 276,000 of its customers. Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models remain the most widely used in the survey, responsible for nearly a third of all proposed code changes submitted for review. More importantly, spending on those tools has grown 10x since the beginning of the year, with their cost now equal to about 2% of total engineering cost. “Even if you’re saying 2% is still small, that 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn’t plan for,” Nicholas Arcolano, the chief scientist at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. We’re certainly getting to the point where people are realizing, okay, it’s not enough to just spend a bunch. You now have to optimize it, make it work.” Anthropic’s new reports speak to that challenge. Anthropic leads among enterprise customers, but what makes an agentic coding tool truly sticky is difficult to identify. The release of OpenAI’s Astra model this summer seemed like a potential threat to Anthropic, but so far it hasn’t slowed Anthropic’s adoption numbers. “It took a long time for us to see Codex really pop in our data at all, and it has come up with Astra [OpenAI’s latest model],” Nikolas Albarran, the AI product lead at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an incumbent weight of their own—this stuff just worked and worked well, and a lot of people just put a lot of effort into standardizing workflows around it. And there’s not a big enough reason to switch.” It’s not just a question of models and workflows, either. The realities of business mean that once a frontier lab has gotten its hooks into a customer, switching is harder than it is compared to an individual programmer or small organization. Albarran points to the investment all the major AI labs are making in forward-deployed engineering (FDE) organizations, teams that embed AI consultants inside customer organizations to help them get off the ground. AI Product.titleZh: Dalet Labs Raises $7 Million for Shopping App Scene: Pitch Deck - Business Insider
AI Product.content: Would you shop from a feed of AI-generated images? The startup Dalet Labs is betting you will. The AI-commerce company exclusively told CMO Insider that it raised a $7 million pre-seed round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and is launching its first product, a shopping app called Scene. Founded by Omer Bar-Tal in 2025 after he left the AI video startup Runway, Dalet Labs recently came out of stealth mode. The startup raised its pre-seed in late 2025, before finalizing its product road map. In addition to Lightspeed, venture capital firm SV Angel and individual angel investors participated in the round. Lisa Han, the Lightspeed partner who led the round, said that Bar-Tal has a combination of "video AI research expertise" and a "deep understanding of what consumers want." Scene, which became available on the Apple App Store in the US on Wednesday, lets people scroll through a feed of shoppable AI-generated images. The app will be invite-only at launch, and isn't yet available on Android. While the images of people or scenes are AI-generated, the products themselves come from real brands across categories like fashion, home decor, and sports. Bar-Tal envisions Scene as a tool people can turn to when they want to buy something but are still uncertain about exactly what they have in mind. It's similar to scrolling through Pinterest or TikTok in hopes of being inspired to buy something, but Bar-Tal said there's a key difference: You come to Scene to shop, not be entertained. Bar-Tal sees Scene as a virtual "mall" where users can window-shop, save items to their cart, and make purchases. Commerce has become an increasingly attractive use case for AI tools like chatbots and agents (including Meta's Muse). However, Bar-Tal argues that AI shopping tools are missing something. "AI is amazing when you know what you want, but it's really important to actually have an ability to discover and to see things," Bar-Tal said. Agentic commerce, he added, "misses the point in shopping — which is essentially a delightful experience." As a Scene user scrolls and interacts with products linked in the app, the feed adapts to what type of brands or items the user is interested in. Then, Scene uses AI to generate scenes with people wearing or using those items. Bar-Tal did not comment on which third-party models Dalet Labs uses. Bar-Tal said Dalet Labs doesn't see its product as replacing influencers, but rather as "complementary." "The content here is AI, but it is not aiming to replace creators because we are not aiming to create entertainment," he said. However, even if Scene isn't competing with influencers for entertaining content, it's still competing with their business model: making money by promoting brands' products and ultimately driving sales. Scene has a catalog of hundreds of brands and retailers, Bar-Tal said, and is making more partnerships. The company did not share further details on what brands Dalet Labs has already established relationships with. Bar-Tal said the company is also leveraging affiliate marketing to monetize the app early on, working with affiliate networks to earn from each in-app transaction. Dalet Labs' Scene is entering a crowded market of apps offering people ways to discover brands and goods, like TikTok's growing Shop presence in the US or Pinterest's visual search prowess. Startups like Doji and Alta have also raised millions on the promise of tech that lets people try on clothes using AI-generated versions of themselves. How will Dalet Labs get people to download an entirely new app? Using influencers and social media to promote the app will be a core part of Dalet Labs' user acquisition plan. It also plans to roll out a coupon campaign during the holidays, offering new users discounts on purchases made through the Scene app. Bar-Tal didn't share whether the discounts would be funded by Scene or by brand partners. Ndoc combines analysis, document writing and presentation building in one product, organized into Stage, Narrative and Model tabs that expose the datasets and Python scripts behind each output. Built on open-source models with a three-person team and no outside funding, the startup is running an enterprise pilot and a limited alpha, and plans a beta within weeks and a full launch next year. Patel also intends to open-source a browser-readable .ndoc.html file format. His exit follows other senior departures from Meta, and Ndoc enters a field where OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta itself are already selling enterprise AI tools. ##### Key Elements ![Meta AI Director Rohit Patel Exits After Eight Years to Launch Ndoc, an AI-Native Rival to Microsoft Office and Google Workspace](https://img.biggo.com/Uj-Jmf6kJ0I07PZuWlmX_ptC8mwc--du2w4wGgt9gFw/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzMwYTQwM2ZkLTliNzktNGE2NC1hZWQ5LTgxMDhhMzE0ZDBhZl8xNzkzMjEzNjI1X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Rohit Patel, a former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has left the company after eight years to start Ndoc, a workspace platform built around AI that is aimed squarely at Microsoft Office and Google Workspace. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) ![Survival LLM runs an AI emergency library with the internet off](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fsurvival-llm-runs-an-ai-emergency-library-with-the-internet-off-1_1793196161001-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # Survival LLM runs an AI emergency library with the internet off • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •7 min read Share this article Survival LLM is a free, open-source desktop app that pairs a local AI model with about 930,000 articles of medical, repair and survival guidance, so it keeps answering when the network goes down. Survival LLM, a free desktop app, answers emergency questions from a library of about 930,000 articles stored on your own machine, with no internet connection required. Ask it how to keep food safe during a blackout, treat a burn or purify water, and it replies from references such as FEMA, the CDC and medical encyclopedias. Every answer names the articles it read, and a click opens the source with the exact passage highlighted. ## The gap it fills Emergency guidance lives on websites, and websites need a network. Cell towers congest during storms and regional outages, and the page that tells you whether chicken is still safe after four hours without power sits on a server you cannot reach. People end up guessing on the questions where guessing costs the most. Survival LLM moves the answers onto the hard drive. The AI model and the reference library both live on your computer, so the app keeps working after you turn the internet off. The developers describe the setup order plainly: install it while you are online, then it needs nothing. Nothing you type leaves the machine. The app asks for no account and runs no tracking. ## What it does Three behaviors separate it from a chatbot that happens to run offline. First, it works with no internet because both the model and the corpus sit on local disk, not on a server behind an API. Second, it cites. Each answer lists the articles behind it. Click a citation and the article opens at the relevant passage, highlighted, so you can check the machine instead of trusting it. Third, it searches rather than recalls when the question demands it. Since version 0.3.4, released Oct. 27, 2026, answers state whether they came from the model's memory, from articles it read, or from search results it did not open. Ask it to look something up and it searches the library even if it answered from memory the first time. ## The library The app bundles plain-text copies of openly licensed and public-domain references, searchable in a fraction of a second: * About 930,000 of Wikipedia's most-read articles * WikiMed medical encyclopedia and MedlinePlus from the U.S. National Library of Medicine * WikEM emergency medicine and UK Medicines A to Z * [Ready.gov](https://www.ready.gov) emergency guides from FEMA and [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov) travelers' health * U.S. military medicine and survival manuals * Risk references for estimating micromorts, including life tables and U.S. death rates * [wikiHow](https://www.wikihow.com) how-to guides and [iFixit](https://www.ifixit.com) repair guides * Appropedia, plus home repair, cooking, gardening, outdoor and ham radio questions from Stack Exchange Each source keeps its own license, and the app shows that license with every article. Some material allows non-commercial use only, which the app surfaces per item. You can add your own files: PDFs, Word documents, ebooks and notes, such as a generator manual or a family emergency plan. The AI searches those too, and they stay on your computer. ## Picking a model The app checks your machine's memory when it opens and downloads the model that fits. More memory buys a smarter model, and the same app binary runs everywhere. | Your computer | Model it downloads | Score on our test | Model size | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Mac with 128 GB or more ...

Excerpted, level-adjusted and faded for this video.* Great product ideas can come from anywhere, but turning them into something tangible often takes time and specialized skills. Replica makes it easier for designers, product managers, and engineers to explore ideas together, get feedback earlier, and iterate without starting from scratch. Unlike generic AI prototyping tools, Replica uses your team’s existing components, patterns, and documentation to guide what gets created. Designers define the guidance, while anyone on the team can use natural language in the GitHub Copilot app to create and refine prototypes that reflect how your product actually works. ### [What can you do with Replica?](#what-can-you-do-with-replica) * **Prototype with your design system:** Use your existing components, patterns, and documentation to guide AI-generated prototypes. * **Turn ideas into interactive experiences:** Describe what you want to explore in natural language, then see, test, and refine the result alongside your Copilot conversation. * **Collaborate and gather feedback:** Publish prototypes to an optional, self-hosted Replica Hub where teammates can explore them and leave comments. * **Adapt Replica to your team:** Customize the open-source tooling and guidance to fit your product and workflows. Replica helps teams move from conversations to tangible experiences faster, so they can test assumptions, explore possibilities, and make better-informed product decisions together. ### [Get started](#get-started) Replica is available now as an open-source project under the MIT license. You can start prototyping locally or set up Replica Hub to share prototypes with your team. Explore the repository for setup instructions, documentation, and examples. Explore [Replica on GitHub](https://github.com/github/replica). We’re excited to share what we’ve been building at GitHub Design and see what the community creates with it. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) ![GitHub developers pushed code 17.9 billion times in 2026 as AI agents reshape how software gets built](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fgithub-developers-pushed-code-179-billion-times-in-2026-as-ai-agents-reshape-how-software-gets-built-2_1793205452479.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #Dev # GitHub developers pushed code 17.9 billion times in 2026 as AI agents reshape how software gets built • ![Marta Kowalska](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Fmarta-kowalska.webp&w=64&q=75) [Marta Kowalska](/author/marta-kowalska) •11 min read Share this article GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report shows developer activity more than tripled in two years, with AI coding agents now starting over 40% of pull requests and developers spreading work across 47 different models. Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the 12 months ending September 30, 2026 — more than the previous two years combined. Commits across public and private repositories climbed to 34.3 billion, over three times the 2024 total. Merged pull requests topped 1.3 billion, averaging 3.5 million per day. The surge coincides with a fundamental shift in how developers work. AI coding agents moved from experimental tools to daily drivers. Repositories created this year with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as new repositories without one. By September, agents started more than 40% of pull requests, up from 17% in March. "The first move is now directing an agent, and review is how developers shape what comes back," said GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke in the report. ### Agents change the rhythm GitHub Actions ran a job 1,440 times every second this year — 124 million per day, more than three times 2025's volume. Developers merged over 30 million Dependabot pull requests to update dependencies, double last year's pace. Activity climbed steadily from January, then surged around June. That inflection point aligns with several industry shifts: more capable underlying models, better tooling around them, and agents that persist across days and orchestrate other specialized agents. Agents also began executing work in the cloud, not just on local machines. From June onward, about 55% of all commits came from brand-new repositories. But veteran developers stayed active. Contributors who pushed code in the past year have been on GitHub for an average of 36 months. Of those who opened a pull request in August, more than 75% pushed code again in September. The average developer now works across 10% more repositories than a year ago. Public contributions soared to 2.5 billion, more than double 2025's 1.12 billion. Maintainers like @kinlane contributed over 1 million times using agentic workflows to keep a machine-readable catalog of public API information current. @kim-em made more than 178,000 contributions maintaining mathlib, a community library of computer-checked mathematics. @andig, maintainer of the open-source EV charging controller evcc, contributed over 21,000 times. ### Developer population grows faster than projected GitHub now serves more than 225 million developers. The United States (38.3 million) and India (32 million) remain the largest communities, each adding over 10 million developers this year. Brazil added 3.28 million, the third-most of any country. Last year GitHub projected India would reach 57.5 million developers by 2030 and the United States 54.7 million. One year into that five-year window, every projected country has already closed at least a fifth of the distance to its 2030 figure. The United States has closed 38.6%; India 28.3%. Forecasting models now diverge sharply. GitHub ran more than 40 models projecting to 2031. About half predict "extreme" growth — more than tripling. Just under half predict "substantial" growth — doubling to tripling. Only three models show modest growth under 2x. The spread reflects how much the 2026 surge widened what seems plausible. Infra & Chips.content: # Oracle Expands Nvidia AI Chip Deal, Adds Google, Cerebras and SambaNova as Capex Targets $95 Billion Rajani Baburajan Oracle is expanding its artificial intelligence infrastructure partnership with Nvidia to multi-gigawatt scale while adding AI processors from Google, Cerebras Systems and SambaNova Systems to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The strategy aims to strengthen Oracle’s position in the global AI cloud market by offering customers more choices for AI model training, inference and enterprise AI applications. Oracle’s AI Chip Strategy The announcement, made on October 27, 2026, represents a significant expansion of Oracle’s AI infrastructure strategy as technology companies accelerate investments in data centers, AI processors and cloud computing. Oracle is also targeting capital expenditure of $90 billion to $95 billion in fiscal 2027, highlighting the substantial investment required to support demand for AI computing capacity. The company has not disclosed the financial value of its expanded Nvidia agreement or the planned purchases from other AI chip suppliers. Oracle and Nvidia Expand AI Infrastructure to Multi-Gigawatt Scale Oracle and Nvidia are expanding their partnership to deploy Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin AI computing systems across OCI Superclusters. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has previously indicated that Vera Rubin systems could generate $40 billion in Nvidia revenue for every gigawatt of deployment. Oracle and Nvidia have also announced the general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs on OCI. Each NVL72 rack connects 72 GPUs through Nvidia’s NVLink technology, while Oracle’s networking architecture supports infrastructure scaling across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. Oracle plans to introduce [Nvidia HGX Rubin NVL8 systems](https://www.oracle.com/news/announcement/ai-world-nvidia-and-oracle-expand-nvidia-vera-rubin-to-multi-gigawatt-scale-2026-10-27/) featuring eight Rubin GPUs, two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 processors, 4 TB of DDR5 memory and 6.4 Tbps networking. The smaller configuration will give enterprises an alternative to large rack-scale deployments for AI training, fine-tuning and inference. Oracle Adds Google TPU Chips to Challenge Nvidia’s Dominance Oracle is diversifying its AI infrastructure by introducing Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) developed by Google. The agreement will make Oracle Cloud Infrastructure the first hyperscale cloud platform outside Google Cloud to offer Google’s TPU technology. Google’s eighth-generation TPU portfolio includes processors optimized for different AI workloads. The TPU 8t architecture targets large-scale AI model training, while TPU 8i focuses on inference workloads, including applications involving multiple AI agents. Oracle expects Google’s TPU offerings to become available on OCI in 2027. The partnership will allow customers to select between Nvidia GPUs and Google TPUs according to their AI computing requirements. For enterprise customers, the availability of alternative processors could improve infrastructure flexibility and create opportunities to optimize AI computing costs. The arrangement could also help organizations run AI applications closer to their existing Oracle databases, reducing the need to transfer enterprise data between cloud environments. However, actual cost savings will depend on processor pricing, application compatibility, utilization and workload performance. Cerebras Partnership Targets High-Speed AI Inference Oracle is also partnering with Cerebras Systems to introduce high-speed AI inference services on OCI. Cerebras specializes in wafer-scale computing technology designed to accelerate AI model execution. Its Wafer-Scale Engine integrates computing and memory resources on a single large processor, reducing the movement of data between separate chips. Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 1 minRead # Oracle Cloud to offer Google TPUs and new AI chips Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) plans to deploy Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and AI inference chips from several providers. This move expands OCI's AI compute options beyond Nvidia GPUs. Google TPUs will be available on OCI in 2027. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 28, 2026 at 09:51 PM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Oracle Cloud to integrate Google TPUs for AI training and inference by 2027. * OCI expands AI chip offerings with OpenAI, Cerebras, SambaNova, and Positron AI. * Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now available on OCI. * OCI Superclusters plan multi-gigawatt expansion using Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. [Oracle Cloud](/tag/oracle+cloud) Infrastructure ([OCI](/tag/oci)) plans to deploy Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and AI inference chips from [OpenAI](/tag/openai), [Cerebras](/tag/cerebras), [SambaNova](/tag/sambanova), and [Positron AI](/tag/positron+ai). This expansion offers OCI customers more options for running AI workloads, moving beyond a primary reliance on [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) GPUs. Oracle announced on Tuesday, October 27, that it will be the first hyperscaler to offer TPUs outside Google Cloud, with availability on OCI in 2027. The announcement, made at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, coincided with an expanded partnership with Nvidia. Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now generally available on OCI. Oracle also plans to scale OCI Superclusters to multi-gigawatt capacity using Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. ### New AI Accelerators Positron AI’s Positron Atlas inference chip is now generally available on OCI. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine for high-speed AI inference is slated for deployment in 2027. Oracle also plans to deploy OpenAI’s Jalapeño inference accelerators, developed with Broadcom, though no specific OCI availability date was provided. SambaNova is collaborating with Oracle to deploy its SN50 inference chips in OCI, with no availability date specified. Industry analysts noted that Oracle's adoption of these additional AI accelerators provides customers with greater flexibility. It allows them to match infrastructure to specific workload requirements, aligning with industry trends towards heterogeneous computing. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

Infra & Chips.content: # citybiz+ Simplismart Raises $14M to Expand AI Inference Infrastructure ### San Francisco-based Simplismart raised $14 million in Series B funding led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The company develops software that helps enterprises optimize AI inference costs, latency, and GPU utilization across cloud and on-premises infrastructure. Customers include HeyGen, Higgsfield and Shiprocket. Simplismart reported 14-fold growth in annualized revenue run rate over six months, as it expands its platform and international cloud partnerships. ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Simplismart.png) San Francisco-based [**Simplismart**](https://simplismart.ai/) has **raised $14 million in a Series B round led by Dallas Venture Capital,** with participation from **Nvidia, Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax** as the AI inference infrastructure company seeks to reduce the cost of running artificial intelligence models in production, shifting attention from model development toward the computing infrastructure required to deliver AI applications reliably at scale. Simplismart develops software that sits between AI models and graphics processing units (GPUs), handling model deployment, performance optimization and ongoing operations. Its inference engine evaluates configurations against requirements such as latency, throughput and cost, while its orchestration platform manages workloads across cloud providers, geographic regions and on-premises infrastructure. “The industry has spent years pushing the limits of what AI models can do. With frontier-class open models now readily available, access alone is no longer enough to set a business apart. The advantage comes from how you run them: what each interaction costs, how quickly the application responds, and whether it stays reliable as demand grows,” said **[Amritanshu Jain](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jainamritanshu/),** co-founder and CEO of Simplismart. Jain is an Indian technology entrepreneur. He earned a Bachelor of Engineering degree from Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS), Pilani. Before launching Simplismart, Jain worked as a machine learning engineer at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, developing cloud and machine learning systems, and at Capillary Technologies, where he contributed to machine learning applications and production-scale data infrastructure. As companies adopt open-weight models and build applications around generative AI, operating costs can become a significant constraint. Simplismart said its software is designed to help enterprises and cloud providers manage GPU resources, balance response times against operating costs, and scale deployments without independently configuring every environment. The company serves customers in video generation, voice, multimodal applications and enterprise software, including HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema. Simplismart also helps cloud infrastructure companies seeking to monetize computing capacity without building their own inference software. Its model differs from businesses that purchase or reserve GPU capacity for resale because it provides the software layer that lets third-party cloud operators offer managed AI services under their own brands. Dallas Venture Capital (DVC) is a venture capital firm with offices in Dallas and Hyderabad that invests in software-as-a-service, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, data, DevOps, and artificial intelligence. Since 2021, DVC has operated its second fund alongside the DVC India Fund. The firm reports $121 million in cumulative capital deployed and 24 investments, with its investment strategy spanning technology companies serving enterprise markets. ## Clients who trust citybiz ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Lime-Logo.png "Lime Logo") ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Sothebys.jpg "Sothebys") ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/202...
